clinicalScope: Diamond‑Blackfan anemia in infants and young children in low‑resource East African hospitals
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A rare congenital erythroid‑lineage failure presenting in infancy with macrocytic anaemia, physical anomalies and a risk of bone‑marrow failure. Diagnosis relies on blood counts, reticulocyte count and exclusion of other causes. Management centres on transfusion, erythropoietin and, if needed, stem‑cell transplant.

sections.p: Diamond‑Blackfan anemia (DBA) is an inherited bone‑marrow failure syndrome characterised by isolated erythroid hypoplasia.
Severity is graded by haemoglobin level and transfusion dependence.
Genetic mutations in ribosomal protein genes (RPS19, RPL5, RPL11) are most common.
b: De novo mutations in ~50% of cases

t.b: Confirms diagnosis and informs family counselling

sections.p: Classic triad: macrocytic anaemia, physical anomalies and growth retardation.
Work‑up focuses on ruling out other causes of anaemia and confirming DBA.
Complications arise from chronic transfusion and disease progression.
Treatment aims to maintain haemoglobin, minimise transfusion burden and address complications.
b: Supportive care: folic acid, infection prophylaxis

sections.p: Regular monitoring of blood counts, iron status and growth is essential.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia with Hb <6 g/dL and signs of hypoxia
Signs of iron overload (hepatomegaly, cardiac dysfunction)

faq.q: Why is reticulocyte count low in DBA?
faq.a: Because erythroid precursors are absent, so few new red cells are released.

faq.q: Can DBA be treated with steroids?
faq.a: No; steroids are ineffective as the defect is in erythroid progenitors.

faq.q: What is the role of genetic counselling?
faq.a: It informs recurrence risk and guides family planning.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in an infant with suspected DBA? — CBC with reticulocyte count; low retic confirms ineffective erythropoiesis.
How would you differentiate DBA from congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia? — Look for dyserythropoiesis on smear; DBA shows normal morphology.
Why is iron chelation indicated in some DBA patients? — Chronic transfusions cause iron overload; ferritin >800 ng/mL triggers chelation.
What is the mainstay of treatment for transfusion‑dependent DBA? — Allogeneic stem‑cell transplant; it is curative.
Why is erythropoietin used in DBA? — It stimulates erythroid progenitors, reducing transfusion needs.
What complication is most feared with long‑term transfusion? — Iron overload leading to organ damage.
When is a bone‑marrow aspirate essential? — To confirm erythroid hypoplasia and exclude other marrow failures.
